verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} another{H312} messenger{H4397} descending{H3381} from the heavens{H8064}, and clothed{H3847} in one{H259} cloud{H6051}, and a bow{H7198} upon his head{H7218}, and his appearance{H4758} like the sun{H8121}, and his feet{H7272} like a flame{H3852} of fire{H784}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַרְאֵיהוּ (mar'ehu — 'his appearance/vision', H4758) — the specific Ezekiel vision word (Ezek 1:5,13,16,26,27,28, 8:2, 40:3, 43:3). Greek has τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ('his face'). A back-translator from Greek would use פָּנָיו (panav — 'his face'), not the Ezekiel-specific mar'eh. The Hebrew describes the angel's total visual impression, not just his face.

Uses כְּלַהֶבֶת אֵשׁ ('like a flame of fire', H3852) — lahevet is the word for the flame of the burning bush (Exodus 3:2 — לַהַבַּת אֵשׁ). Greek has ὡς στύλοι πυρός ('as pillars of fire'), echoing the Exodus wilderness pillar instead. A back-translator from Greek would write כְּעַמּוּדֵי אֵשׁ ('like pillars of fire'), not the burning-bush term. The Hebrew connects the angel's feet to the theophany at the bush; the Greek translator substituted the pillar of cloud and fire — different Exodus imagery entirely.

Uses קֶשֶׁת (qeshet — 'bow', H7198) — the same word for God's covenant bow set in the clouds after the Flood (Gen 9:13-16: אֶת קַשְׁתִּי נָתַתִּי בֶּעָנָן — 'I have set my bow in the cloud'). Greek has ἶρις ('rainbow/iris'). The Hebrew word is loaded with Noahic covenant theology — this is THE bow of the covenant, not merely a rainbow. A back-translator from Greek ἶρις would not naturally reach for the Genesis covenant term.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἰσχυρόν ('mighty/strong') to describe the angel — absent from the Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'his appearance like the sun' (total visual impression). Greek: 'his face as the sun' (only the face).
Hebrew: 'like a flame of fire' (burning bush imagery). Greek: 'as pillars of fire' (wilderness pillar imagery). Different Exodus echoes.
translation_notes: 'Appearance' for mar'ehu rather than 'face' — preserving the broader visual sense and the Ezekiel vision-vocabulary connection.
'Bow' for qeshet rather than 'rainbow' — preserving the Genesis 9 covenant terminology. The angel bears the covenant sign in the cloud.

'One cloud' — the Hebrew specifies אֶחָד (echad), which may function as an intensifier or indefinite article in later Hebrew, but may also emphasize the singularity/unity of the cloud wrapping the angel.
textual_notes: The angel's description combines creation and covenant imagery: clothed in a cloud (Exodus theophany, Ex 13:21, 19:9), bearing the covenant bow (Genesis 9), with burning-bush flame feet (Exodus 3:2). This is a composite OT divine-presence portrait that no back-translator would independently assemble.

verses.translation: And in his hand{H3027} one{H259} scroll{H5612}, open{H6605}; and he trod{H1869} with his right{H3225} foot{H7272} upon the sea{H3220}, and with his left{H8040} upon the dry-land{H3004}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סֵפֶר (sefer — 'scroll/document', H5612) — the standard OT word for a written document (Deut 24:1; Isa 29:11-12; Jer 32:10-12). Greek has βιβλαρίδιον (biblaridion — 'little book'), a Greek diminutive. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate or use סֵפֶר קָטָן ('small scroll'), not the unmodified sefer. The Hebrew never uses a diminutive — this is simply a scroll, the same word used for the Torah scroll, the scroll of the covenant, and Jeremiah's scroll.

CRITICAL: Uses יַבָּשָׁה (yabashah — 'the dry-land', H3004) — the specific creation word from Genesis 1:9-10 (וַיִּקְרָא אֱלֹהִים לַיַּבָּשָׁה אֶרֶץ — 'and God called the dry-land earth'). Greek uses γῆ (ge — 'earth/land'). A back-translator from Greek would use אֶרֶץ (erets — 'earth/land'), not the Genesis creation term. The angel stands on the sea and the dry-land — the two domains separated at creation. This creation vocabulary appears three times in this chapter (vv. 2, 5, 8).

Uses דָּרַךְ (darakh — 'trod/stepped', H1869) — the verb for treading on high places (Deut 33:29), treading the winepress (Isa 63:3, Mic 1:3), and bending the bow in conquest (Jer 51:3). Greek has ἔθηκε (etheke — 'placed/set'). The Hebrew verb implies authority and dominion — one treads upon what one rules over. A back-translator from Greek 'placed' would use שָׂם (sam — 'put') or הִנִּיחַ (hiniach — 'set down'), not the dominion verb darakh.
greek_deviations: Greek: βιβλαρίδιον ('little book' — diminutive). Hebrew: סֵפֶר ('scroll'). Greek uses a diminutive absent from Hebrew.
Greek: ἔθηκε ('placed/set'). Hebrew: דָּרַךְ ('trod'). Different verbs with different connotations — neutral placement vs. authoritative treading.
translation_notes: 'Trod' for darakh captures the Hebrew verb's connotation of dominion and authority — the angel exercises rule over sea and land.
'Dry-land' for yabashah preserves the Genesis 1 creation distinction from erets ('earth'). The sea-and-dry-land pairing is creation vocabulary.
textual_notes: The sea-and-dry-land pairing recalls Genesis 1:9-10 and Jonah 1:9 where Jonah declares: 'I fear YHWH, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry-land (הַיַּבָּשָׁה).' The angel stands as lord over the two creation domains.

verses.translation: And he cried out{H6817} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963}, like the cry{H6817} of the lion{H738}. And in the hour that he cried out{H6817}, seven{H7651} voices{H6963} were speaking{H1696} in their voices{H6963}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses צָעַק (tsa'aq — 'cried out', H6817) for the angel's voice, not שָׁאַג (sha'ag — 'roared') which is THE standard Hebrew word for a lion's roar (Amos 3:4,8; Hos 11:10; Joel 4:16). Greek has ἔκραξε ('cried out'). A back-translator could choose either verb, but the author's deliberate choice of tsa'aq — the verb of the Exodus cry for deliverance (Ex 2:23, 14:10; Judg 3:9,15, 4:3, 6:6) — reframes the angel's lion-cry as a cry that initiates deliverance, not a roar of dominance.

Uses קוֹלוֹת (qolot — 'voices', H6963) where Greek has βρονταί ('thunders'). The Hebrew word is the same as the 'thunderings' at Sinai (Ex 19:16 — קֹלֹת וּבְרָקִים, 'thunderings and lightnings'; Ex 20:18 — the people saw the קוֹלֹת). At Sinai, divine voice and thunder were indistinguishable — the qolot were simultaneously God's speech and heaven's thunder. A back-translator from Greek βρονταί ('thunders') would use רְעָמִים (re'amim — 'thunders'), not the theologically loaded, Sinai-specific qolot.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'seven thunders uttered their voices' (ἑπτὰ βρονταί). Hebrew: 'seven voices speaking in their voices' (שבעה קולות). The Hebrew maintains the Sinai ambiguity between divine speech and thunder.
Greek: ἐλάλησαν ('uttered/spoke'). Hebrew: מְדַבְּרִים ('speaking' — pi'el participle of דבר). The Hebrew uses a continuous participle (ongoing speech), not a completed action.
translation_notes: 'Voices' for qolot preserves the Hebrew ambiguity: at Sinai, God's 'voices' WERE the 'thunders' (Ex 19:16, 20:18; Ps 29). The seven voices both speak and thunder simultaneously.

שָׁעָה (sha'ah) as 'hour' is a later Hebrew/Aramaic temporal word (cf. Dan 3:6, 4:16), indicating the text's linguistic register. In biblical Hebrew the root שעה (H8159) means 'to gaze/look' — the 'hour' meaning reflects Second Temple usage.
textual_notes: The lion comparison echoes Amos 3:8 — 'The lion has roared (שָׁאַג), who will not fear? The Lord YHWH has spoken, who can but prophesy?' — which directly precedes the Amos 3:7 quotation appearing in verse 7 of this chapter. The Hebrew author draws on Amos 3 as a sequential source unit: lion cry (v3), divine counsels revealed to prophets (v7).

verses.translation: And after{H310} they spoke{H1696} in their voices{H6963}, I desired{H7521} to write{H3789} them. I heard{H8085} a heavenly-voice from the heavens{H8064}, the one saying{H559} to me: Seal{H5640} them and do not write{H3789}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בַּת קוֹל (bat qol — literally 'daughter of a voice') — the uniquely Jewish/rabbinic term for a heavenly voice, a diminished echo of divine speech. This is a technical Hebrew idiom with no Greek equivalent. Greek has φωνὴν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ('a voice from heaven'). A back-translator from Greek would NEVER produce bat qol — they would write קוֹל מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם ('a voice from heaven'). Bat qol is a concept embedded in Hebrew/Aramaic thought: a 'daughter' (echo/derivative) of the original divine voice that ceased with the last prophets. This appears twice in this chapter (vv. 4, 8) and is among the strongest one-way markers in the entire Hebrew Revelation.

Uses רָצִיתִי (ratsiti — 'I desired/wanted', H7521) — a verb of inner will and desire. Greek has ἔμελλον γράφειν ('I was about to write'). The Hebrew describes Yochanan's psychological state (desire to write); the Greek describes his impending action (about to write). A back-translator from Greek would use עָמַדְתִּי ל... ('I was about to...') or הָיִיתִי עָתִיד ('I was going to'), not the desire verb ratsah.

הָאוֹמֶרֶת (ha'omeret) — feminine participle, grammatically agreeing with the feminine bat qol. This natural gender agreement demonstrates the author thinks in Hebrew. A back-translator would not need to produce this specifically feminine participial form to match the technical bat qol idiom.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'I desired to write' (רציתי — psychological state). Greek: 'I was about to write' (ἔμελλον — impending action).
Hebrew: bat qol (technical rabbinic concept). Greek: generic 'voice from heaven.'
translation_notes: 'Heavenly-voice' for bat qol captures the technical meaning without the literal 'daughter of a voice.' The bat qol in Jewish tradition is a diminished form of prophecy — an echo of the divine voice.
'Desired' for ratsiti — the Hebrew emphasizes that Yochanan WANTED to write, not merely that he was about to. His will was overridden by divine command.
textual_notes: Daniel 8:26 and 12:4,9 use סָתַם (satam — 'seal up', H5640) for concealing prophetic content until the appointed time. The command to 'seal' rather than 'write' connects directly to Daniel's sealed visions — same verb, same concept of restricted revelation.

verses.translation: And the messenger{H4397} standing{H5975} upon the sea{H3220} and upon the dry-land{H3004}, whom I saw{H7200}, raised{H7311} his right{H3225} and his left{H8040} to the heavens{H8064}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has 'raised his right AND his left to the heavens' — BOTH hands raised. Greek has τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ ('his hand' — SINGULAR). A back-translator from Greek would write יָרֶם יָדוֹ ('raised his hand,' singular). The Hebrew's two-hands posture follows Daniel 12:7 EXACTLY: וַיָּרֶם יְמִינוֹ וּשְׂמֹאלוֹ אֶל הַשָּׁמַיִם ('and he raised his right hand and his left hand to the heavens'). The Hebrew copies Daniel's angel gesture with precision; the Greek reduces it to a standard one-hand oath. No back-translator from Greek would independently recover the Daniel 12:7 two-hand detail.

Second occurrence of יַבָּשָׁה (yabashah, H3004 — 'dry-land'). The sustained use of the Genesis 1 creation term throughout the chapter (vv. 2, 5, 8) is a deliberate literary pattern, not a coincidence a back-translator would reproduce three times.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: both hands raised (יְמִינוֹ וּשְׂמֹאלוֹ — 'his right and his left'). Greek: one hand raised (τὴν χεῖρα — 'the hand,' singular).
translation_notes: The brackets [ ] in the source text indicate a lacuna — a gap where text was lost or illegible. The surrounding syntax flows coherently without the missing material.
textual_notes: Daniel 12:7 — 'And I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river: he raised his right hand and his left hand to the heavens and swore by the Living-One of eternity.' The Hebrew Revelation follows Daniel's angel with precision: both hands raised (v5), same oath formula (v6). The Greek Revelation follows Daniel less closely by reducing to a single hand.

verses.translation: And he swore{H7650} by the Living-One{H2416} of eternity{H5769}, the Creator{H1254} of the heavens{H8064} and what is in it, and the earth{H776} and the sea{H3220} and all{H3605} that is in them, that there is no more{H5750} time{H6256}.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT PARALLEL to Daniel 12:7: וַיִּשָּׁבַע בְּחֵי הָעוֹלָם ('and he swore by the Living-One of eternity'). The Hebrew oath formula is identical to Daniel's. Greek has ὤμοσεν ἐν τῷ ζῶντι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('swore by the one living unto the ages of the ages'). The Hebrew is a compact oath formula used as a divine title; the Greek is an expanded descriptive phrase. A back-translator from Greek would write בְּחֵי לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים ('by the living one forever and ever'), not the compact Danielic formula בְּחֵי הָעוֹלָם.

Uses הַבֹּרֵא (habore — 'THE Creator', H1254) — a participial divine TITLE with the definite article, from the Genesis 1:1 creation verb בָּרָא (bara). Greek has ὃς ἔκτισε ('who created') — a descriptive relative clause. A back-translator from Greek would write שֶׁבָּרָא ('who created'), not the title form 'the Creator.' The Hebrew treats creation as a divine NAME; the Greek treats it as a divine ACT.

Uses בָּהּ (bah — 'in it,' feminine singular) for the heavens, then בָּהֶם (bahem — 'in them,' masculine plural) for earth and sea. This mixed-gender reference pattern — treating שָׁמַיִם as a feminine collective, then switching to masculine plural — is natural Hebrew. A back-translator from the consistent Greek ἐν αὐτοῖς would use a uniform pronoun throughout.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Creator' (הַבֹּרֵא — participial title). Greek: 'who created' (ὃς ἔκτισε — relative clause). Title vs. description.
Hebrew: 'by the Living-One of eternity' (compact formula). Greek: 'by the one living unto the ages of the ages' (expanded description).
translation_notes: 'The Living-One of eternity' for bechey ha'olam — preserving this as a title/name rather than a description. This is how YHWH is named in Daniel's oath formula.
'The Creator' for habore — preserving the participial title form that makes creation itself a divine name.
textual_notes: Daniel 12:7 full context: 'And I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he raised his right hand and his left hand to the heavens and swore by the Living-One of eternity (בְּחֵי הָעוֹלָם), that it would be for a time, times, and half a time.' Both angels raise both hands and use the same oath formula, but declare different things about time — Daniel's angel sets a duration; this angel declares time's end.
The creation formula (heavens + what's in them, earth, sea + all in them) echoes Exodus 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:6 — liturgical creation confessions used in OT worship.

verses.translation: Only{H7535} when the seven{H7651} messengers{H4397} blow{H8628} on the shofars{H7782}, shall all{H3605} these{H428} be completed{H3615} — the counsels{H5475} of YHWH{H3068} — just as he made known{H3045} to his servants{H5650} and to his prophets{H5030}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שׁוֹפָרוֹת (shofarot — 'shofars/rams' horns', H7782) with תּוֹקְעִים (toq'im — 'blow', H8628). These are the specific Sinai/Jericho/Jubilee terms. At Sinai: 'the voice of the shofar' (Ex 19:16,19, 20:18). At Jericho: 'blow (תָּקַע) on the shofars' (Josh 6:4,8,9,13,16,20). On Yom Kippur: 'you shall blow (תָּקַע) the shofar' (Lev 25:9). Greek uses σαλπίζω/σάλπιγξ ('sound a trumpet'). A back-translator from Greek would use חֲצוֹצְרָה (chatsotsrah — 'metal trumpet') not שׁוֹפָר (ram's horn), and might use a generic verb rather than the technical תָּקַע.

CRITICAL: Uses הַסּוֹדוֹת (hasodot — 'the counsels/secrets', H5475 — PLURAL) of YHWH. Greek has τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ θεοῦ ('the mystery of God' — SINGULAR). Multiple differences: (1) Hebrew plural vs. Greek singular; (2) Hebrew סוֹד (sod — 'counsel/council') vs. Greek μυστήριον ('mystery'); (3) Hebrew YHWH vs. Greek θεός ('God'). The Hebrew סוֹד is the word for YHWH's intimate divine council (Jer 23:18,22; Ps 25:14, 89:8; Job 15:8; Prov 3:32) — the inner circle of divine deliberation. A back-translator from Greek would use רָז (raz — Daniel's Aramaic 'mystery', Dan 2:18-19,27-30,47) or render μυστήριον in some other way, not the OT-specific סוֹד.

NEAR-QUOTE of Amos 3:7: כִּי לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה דָּבָר כִּי אִם גָּלָה סוֹדוֹ אֶל עֲבָדָיו הַנְּבִיאִים — 'For the Lord YHWH does nothing unless he reveals his counsel (sodo) to his servants the prophets.' The Hebrew has: הסודות יהוה כמו שמודיע לעבדיו ולנביאיו — same key vocabulary: סוד + יהוה + עבדים + נביאים. A back-translator from Greek, which lacks all four of these specific Hebrew terms, would not independently reconstruct this Amos quotation.

Hebrew: הַשִּׁבְעָה מַלְאָכִים ('the SEVEN messengers' — cardinal number, all seven). Greek: τοῦ ἑβδόμου ἀγγέλου ('the SEVENTH angel' — ordinal number, one specific angel). A back-translator from Greek would write הַמַּלְאָךְ הַשְּׁבִיעִי ('the seventh messenger'), not הַשִּׁבְעָה מַלְאָכִים ('the seven messengers'). The Hebrew envisions the completion of all seven shofar blasts as a unified event; the Greek isolates the seventh.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the seven messengers' (all seven, cardinal). Greek: 'the seventh angel' (one, ordinal).
Hebrew: 'the counsels' (plural, סוֹדוֹת). Greek: 'the mystery' (singular, μυστήριον).
Hebrew: 'YHWH' (the divine name). Greek: 'God' (θεοῦ).
Hebrew: 'he made known' (neutral הוֹדִיעַ). Greek: 'he declared good news' (εὐηγγέλισεν, from εὐαγγελίζω). The Greek adds a 'good news/gospel' connotation absent from the neutral Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Counsels' for sodot rather than 'mysteries' — preserving the Hebrew concept of divine council deliberation (sod) as distinct from Greek μυστήριον.
'Shofars' rather than 'trumpets' — the shofar is a ram's horn, not a metal trumpet (חֲצוֹצְרָה). The instruments carry entirely different theological weight: Sinai, Jericho, Jubilee, Rosh HaShanah.
textual_notes: Amos 3:7 is the direct OT source for this verse's language. In Amos, the declaration that YHWH reveals his sod to his servants the prophets comes immediately after the lion metaphor (Amos 3:4,8) — the same lion that appears in v3 of this chapter. The Hebrew author works through Amos 3 as a sequential source: lion cry (v3) → divine counsels revealed to prophets (v7).

The feminine plural תִּכְלֶינָה ('shall be completed') agrees with the implied feminine referent — the counsels/events. The messengers are masculine, but the things to be completed are treated as feminine, a natural Hebrew construction.

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} again{H5750} a heavenly-voice saying{H559} to me: Go{H1980} and take{H3947} the scroll{H5612}, the open-one{H6605}, from the hand{H3027} of the messenger{H4397} standing{H5975} upon the sea{H3220} and upon the dry-land{H3004}.

one_way_hebrew: Second occurrence of בַּת קוֹל (bat qol). Here the participle is masculine אֹמֵר (omer) rather than feminine אוֹמֶרֶת (omeret) as in v4. The shift from feminine (agreeing with the grammatically feminine bat qol) to masculine (reflecting the male speaker behind the voice) is a natural Hebrew phenomenon — the author shifts between grammatical agreement and notional agreement. A back-translator from Greek, which has no such gender alternation in the source, would not produce this shift.

Third occurrence of יַבָּשָׁה (yabashah — 'dry-land', H3004). The threefold repetition of the Genesis 1 creation vocabulary throughout the chapter (vv. 2, 5, 8) is a sustained literary pattern that stamps the entire vision with creation theology.
greek_deviations: Greek: βιβλαρίδιον ('little book' — diminutive). Hebrew: סֵפֶר ('scroll'). As in v2, the Hebrew never diminishes the scroll.
The gap marked [ ] in the source text between הספר and הפתוח suggests a word was lost. Greek has no corresponding gap.
translation_notes: The masculine אֹמֵר (omer) after bat qol may indicate the bat kol here serves as the vehicle for a male speaker — possibly YHWH himself speaking through the heavenly voice-echo.

verses.translation: And I went{H1980} to the messenger{H4397} and I said{H559} to him: Give{H5414} me the scroll{H5612}. And he said{H559} to me: Take{H3947} and swallow{H1104} it, and it shall be{H1961} for you like honey{H1706} in your mouth{H6310}, but in your innards{H4578} it shall make{H6213} for you pain.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְּנוּ (tenu — 'give!', PLURAL imperative of natan, H5414) when addressing a single angel. This is the Hebrew honorific plural — using plural address for a being of superior rank, analogous to the majestic plural. Greek has δός μοι (dos moi — 'give me,' singular imperative). A back-translator from the Greek singular imperative would write תֵּן (ten — singular), not the respectful plural. This reveals a Hebrew-speaking author's instinct for polite address to an angelic being.

Uses בוֹלֵעַ (bole'a — 'swallow', H1104) — the verb for swallowing whole, used of the great fish swallowing Jonah (Jonah 2:1) and the earth swallowing Korah (Num 16:30,32,34; Deut 11:6). Greek has κατάφαγε (kataphage — 'eat up/devour'). A back-translator from Greek would use אָכַל (akhal — 'eat') not בָּלַע (bala — 'swallow'). Eating involves chewing and processing; swallowing is whole absorption. The scroll is not to be analyzed (chewed) but internalized whole.

Uses צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'pain/distress') where Greek has πικρανεῖ ('shall make bitter'). A back-translator from Greek would use מַר (mar — 'bitter') or יְמָרֵר (yemarer — 'make bitter'). The Hebrew describes physical pain in the innards; the Greek describes a taste sensation (bitterness). Different bodily experiences entirely.

Uses feminine אוֹתָהּ (otah — 'it,' fem.) for the scroll, though סֵפֶר (sefer) is grammatically masculine. This may reflect the author thinking of the content as תּוֹרָה (torah — feminine) or מְגִלָּה (megillah — 'scroll,' feminine). In v10, the pronoun switches to masculine אוֹתוֹ. This gender oscillation is a natural Hebrew phenomenon that a back-translator from Greek (which uses consistent neuter throughout) would not produce.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'swallow it' (בוֹלֵעַ — swallow whole). Greek: 'eat it up' (κατάφαγε — devour). Different physical actions.
Hebrew: 'it shall make for you pain' (צער — physical suffering). Greek: 'it shall make your belly bitter' (πικρανεῖ — bitterness). Different sensory experience.
Hebrew: 'Give me' (תנו — plural/honorific address to a single angel). Greek: 'Give me' (δός — singular, no honorific).
translation_notes: 'Swallow' for bole'a rather than 'eat' — preserving the Hebrew verb's meaning of whole ingestion without chewing. The prophetic word enters whole.
'Pain' for tsa'ar — later Hebrew for distress/suffering, distinct from the Greek concept of bitterness. Prophecy causes internal pain, not merely a bitter taste.
כִּדְבַשׁ (kidvash — 'like honey') echoes Ezekiel 3:3 where the scroll tastes מָתוֹק כִּדְבַשׁ ('sweet like honey'). Both prophets consume a divine scroll with the same result.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 3:1-3 is the direct OT parallel: 'Son of man, eat this scroll... So I ate it, and it was in my mouth like honey for sweetness.' The Hebrew Revelation follows the Ezekiel scroll-eating pattern closely but adds the element of internal pain — prophecy is sweet to receive but painful to carry.

verses.translation: And I took{H3947} the scroll{H5612} from the hand{H3027} of the messenger{H4397} and swallowed{H1104} it, and it was{H1961} like honey{H1706} in my mouth{H6310}. And after{H310} I ate{H398}, it made{H6213} for me pain in my innards{H4578}.

one_way_hebrew: Now uses masculine אוֹתוֹ (oto — 'it,' masc.) for the scroll, matching the masculine סֵפֶר, after the feminine אוֹתָהּ in v9. This gender oscillation within two consecutive verses is a natural Hebrew phenomenon — the author shifts between thinking of the physical scroll (masc. sefer) and its content (fem. torah/megillah). A back-translator from Greek, which uses consistent neuter τὸ βιβλαρίδιον throughout, would maintain uniform grammatical reference.

Uses two distinct verbs in sequence: בוֹלֵעַ (bole'a — 'swallowed,' H1104) for the initial act, then אָכַלְתִּי (akhalti — 'I ate,' H398) for the completed process. The Hebrew distinguishes swallowing (whole ingestion) from eating (full digestion). Greek uses only κατέφαγον (katephagon — 'ate up') for the action. This lexical distinction is a natural Hebrew feature.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'it made for me pain in my innards' (צער — physical suffering). Greek: 'my belly was made bitter' (ἐπικράνθη — embittered). Same divergence as v9 — pain vs. bitterness.
translation_notes: The two-verb distinction (swallowed → ate) mirrors the prophetic process: the scroll enters whole (swallowing) then is processed through experience (eating). Prophecy is received as complete revelation, then digested through living it out.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to me: You must prophesy{H5012} again{H5750} to nations{H3816} and to peoples{H5971} and to kings{H4428}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses TWO distinct Hebrew words for 'peoples': לְאֻמִּים (le'umim, H3816 — 'nations') AND עַמִּים (amim, H5971 — 'peoples'). These carry different nuances: le'umim emphasizes ethnic/national identity (Gen 25:23, Ps 2:1, Isa 34:1); amim emphasizes communal/social grouping. Greek has λαοῖς ('peoples') and ἔθνεσιν ('nations') PLUS γλώσσαις ('tongues') and βασιλεῦσι ('kings') — a FOUR-fold list vs. the Hebrew THREE-fold list. A back-translator from Greek would include לְשׁוֹנוֹת (leshonot — 'tongues'), which the Hebrew entirely lacks.

Uses צָרִיךְ (tsarikh — 'must/need') — a Mishnaic Hebrew word absent from the biblical corpus. This reveals the author's linguistic register: a Hebrew speaker of the Second Temple period using living vernacular Hebrew, not a translator artificially reconstructing biblical idiom from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three categories (nations, peoples, kings). Greek: four categories (peoples, nations, tongues, kings). Greek adds 'tongues/languages' absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: לְאֻמִּים then עַמִּים (two distinct Hebrew words for 'peoples'). Greek: λαοῖς then ἔθνεσιν — different order and different semantic range.
translation_notes: 'Nations' for le'umim and 'peoples' for amim — preserving the distinction between the two Hebrew terms. Le'umim has a more ethnic/political sense; amim has a more communal/social sense.
צָרִיךְ (tsarikh) as 'must' — characteristic Mishnaic Hebrew indicating obligation/necessity, further evidence of the text's living Hebrew register rather than artificial back-translation.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 1:10 — 'I have appointed you this day over nations (גּוֹיִם) and over kingdoms (מַמְלָכוֹת).' The prophetic commission to address nations and kings echoes the classical prophetic calling. The Hebrew Revelation recommissions Yochanan in the pattern of Jeremiah.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 10 in Hebrew centers on the bat kol (heavenly voice), the scroll-swallowing prophetic commission, and the completion of YHWH's counsels. The chapter contains at least 15 clear one-way translation markers. The most striking are: (1) בַּת קוֹל (bat kol) — the uniquely rabbinic term for a heavenly voice, appearing twice (vv. 4, 8) with no Greek equivalent and no possibility of back-translation; (2) יַבָּשָׁה (yabashah — 'dry-land') — the Genesis 1:9-10 creation term, used three times (vv. 2, 5, 8) where Greek has generic 'earth'; (3) שׁוֹפָרוֹת with תּוֹקְעִים — the Sinai/Jericho/Jubilee vocabulary (v. 7) vs. Greek 'trumpets'; (4) הַסּוֹדוֹת יַהְוֶה... לַעֲבָדָיו וְלִנְבִיאָיו — the near-quote of Amos 3:7 using סוֹד/YHWH/servants/prophets (v. 7), where the Greek has none of these four Hebrew terms; (5) the Daniel 12:7 oath formula בְּחֵי הָעוֹלָם with BOTH hands raised (vv. 5-6) vs. Greek's single hand and expanded phrasing; (6) הַבֹּרֵא as a participial divine title vs. the Greek descriptive clause (v. 6); (7) הַשִּׁבְעָה מַלְאָכִים ('the seven messengers,' cardinal) vs. Greek τοῦ ἑβδόμου ἀγγέλου ('the seventh angel,' ordinal) (v. 7); (8) the plural honorific תְּנוּ addressing a single angel (v. 9); (9) בוֹלֵעַ ('swallow,' the Jonah/Korah verb) vs. Greek 'eat up' (vv. 9-10); (10) צַעַר ('pain') vs. Greek 'bitterness' (vv. 9-10); and (11) the gender oscillation of the scroll pronoun (fem. v9, masc. v10). The chapter's sustained use of yabashah marks the angel as standing on the CREATION domain (sea + dry-land from Genesis 1), while the Amos 3 connection (lion cry in v3 echoing Amos 3:8, divine counsels in v7 quoting Amos 3:7) provides a unified prophetic framework. The Hebrew draws on Daniel 12 for the oath scene and Ezekiel 3 for the scroll-eating, weaving these OT threads into a tapestry that no back-translator from Greek could independently reconstruct.
